<!-- data-checksum: ffc54e2ad996e1e61ad10ca520e4d588 -->

Two groups of **different** patients: a removable boot vs a cast in a trial, hamstring vs BPTB grafts, implant A vs implant C. This is the most common comparison in clinical research. If the same patients are measured twice, or patients were matched in pairs, use [page 7](07-two-paired-groups.qmd) instead.

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 How every section on this page works
Each section answers one question about one of the practice's datasets: a randomized trial of a cast vs a removable boot after a midfoot injury (the t and Mann-Whitney tests), ACL reconstructions (Fisher's test) and the joint replacement cohort (the log-rank test). The trial and its results are invented for teaching. Each section's first code block loads the packages and the data, so you can jump straight to the section you need. Run that section's blocks in order, top to bottom.

To keep the code short, the joint replacement example uses every case, including the 80 patients who had both sides operated on. In a real study, decide how to handle them ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#paired)) and say what you did.
:::

## Unpaired t test {#unpaired-t}

**The question:** Is the EFAS score 3 months after a midfoot injury different with a removable boot than with a cast?

### When to use it

- The outcome is a **measurement**, compared between **two independent groups**.
- Within **each group** it's roughly normal, or each group is large (about 30 or more) and not badly skewed ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#within-groups)).
- A score that adds up several questions, such as the EFAS score (six questions scored 0 to 4, so 0 to 24), can be treated as a measurement when few patients sit at its floor or ceiling.
- Use **Welch's** version, which doesn't assume the two groups have the same spread. It's R's default, but not Python's (see the R vs Python box).
- If the outcome is skewed, piles up at a floor or ceiling, or is ordinal → the [Mann-Whitney test](#mann-whitney).

### Look at the data first

The trial randomized 120 patients, 60 to each arm, and measured the EFAS score (European Foot and Ankle Society; 24 is the best) at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

trial <- read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)   # one row per patient and visit

efas_3mo <- trial |>
  filter(visit == "3mo", !is.na(efas)) |>                  # patients seen at 3 months
  mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("boot", "cast")))    # boot first: differences are boot minus cast

ggplot(efas_3mo, aes(efas)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "EFAS score at 3 months (24 = best)", y = "Patients")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-two-unpaired-groups_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
efas_3mo |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(efas), sd = sd(efas))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  arm       n  mean    sd
  <fct> <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1 boot     57  17.4  2.90
2 cast     55  13.8  3.39
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

trial = pd.read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv")                    # one row per patient and visit
efas_3mo = trial[trial["visit"] == "3mo"].dropna(subset=["efas"])      # patients seen at 3 months
efas_boot = efas_3mo.loc[efas_3mo["arm"] == "boot", "efas"]
efas_cast = efas_3mo.loc[efas_3mo["arm"] == "cast", "efas"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6, 4), sharex=True)
axes[0].hist(efas_boot, bins=range(0, 26))
axes[0].set_title("boot")
axes[1].hist(efas_cast, bins=range(0, 26))
axes[1].set_title("cast")
axes[1].set_xlabel("EFAS score at 3 months (24 = best)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-two-unpaired-groups_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png)
:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(efas_3mo.groupby("arm")["efas"].agg(["count", "mean", "std"]))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      count       mean       std
arm                             
boot     57  17.403509  2.896178
cast     55  13.818182  3.394390
```


:::
:::

:::

Both arms are roughly bell-shaped, with no patient at the floor (0) or the ceiling (24), and both are large. The boot arm sits to the right. Eight patients missed the 3-month visit (3 in the boot arm, 5 in the cast arm), so 112 of the 120 randomized patients are analyzed.

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
efas_test <- t.test(efas ~ arm, data = efas_3mo)   # Welch's t test is R's default
efas_test
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  efas by arm
t = 6.0036, df = 106.05, p-value = 2.738e-08
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group boot and group cast is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.401333 4.769321
sample estimates:
mean in group boot mean in group cast 
          17.40351           13.81818 
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
efas_test = stats.ttest_ind(efas_boot, efas_cast, equal_var=False)   # equal_var=False: Welch's t test
print(efas_test)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
TtestResult(statistic=np.float64(6.003593894847252), pvalue=np.float64(2.7379453104403824e-08), df=np.float64(106.05006461078466))
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(efas_boot.mean() - efas_cast.mean(), efas_test.confidence_interval())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
3.585326953748007 ConfidenceInterval(low=np.float64(2.401332702196515), high=np.float64(4.769321205299499))
```


:::
:::

:::





### Read the output

- **t = 6.00:** the difference between the means is 6 standard errors.
- **df = 106.05:** Welch's test adjusts the degrees of freedom for unequal spreads, so they aren't a whole number.
- **p < 0.001:** a difference this large would be very unlikely if the two arms had the same mean EFAS score.
- **95% CI 2.40 to 4.77:** the CI for the **difference in means**, boot minus cast.
- **mean in group boot 17.4, mean in group cast 13.8:** the two means.

### Effect size and 95% CI

- The **mean difference** with its CI is the effect size readers understand best: 3.6 points (95% CI 2.4 to 4.8).
- **Hedges' g** expresses the difference in standard deviations, which lets you compare effects measured on different scales. As a rough guide, 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
effectsize::hedges_g(efas ~ arm, data = efas_3mo)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Hedges' g |       95% CI
------------------------
1.13      | [0.73, 1.52]

- Estimated using pooled SD.
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
g = pg.compute_effsize(efas_boot, efas_cast, eftype="hedges")
print(g)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
1.130200311478461
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(pg.compute_esci(stat=g, nx=len(efas_boot), ny=len(efas_cast), eftype="hedges", decimals=3))   # its 95% CI
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[0.727 1.534]
```


:::
:::

:::





Hedges' g is 1.13: the boot arm's mean is more than one standard deviation higher, a large effect. Whether 3.6 points on a 24-point score matters to patients is a clinical question, not a statistical one.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** EFAS scores at 3 months were compared between the arms with Welch's unpaired t test, in the patients seen at that visit.
>
> **Results:** At 3 months, the mean EFAS score was 17.4 points (SD 2.9; n = 57) with a boot and 13.8 (SD 3.4; n = 55) with a cast (difference 3.6 points, 95% CI 2.4 to 4.8; Hedges' g = 1.13, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.52; p < 0.001).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: don't test the variances first
An old habit is to run a test of equal variances (such as Levene's) and then choose Student's or Welch's t test depending on the result. Don't: the two-step procedure distorts the p-value. Use Welch's test from the start. When the variances really are equal, it gives almost the same answer as Student's.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: Student's or Welch's?
- **The default differs.** R's `t.test()` runs **Welch's** test unless you add `var.equal = TRUE`. scipy's `ttest_ind()` runs **Student's** test unless you add `equal_var=False`. Always set it explicitly in Python.
- **The order of the groups.** R subtracts in the order of the factor levels (we put boot first); scipy subtracts the second argument from the first.
- **The CI for Hedges' g.** effectsize uses an exact method and pingouin an approximation, so the CIs can differ slightly (0.73 to 1.52 in R, 0.73 to 1.53 in Python). The estimates agree to five decimals: both correct g for small samples, effectsize with the exact formula and pingouin with the usual approximation.
:::

## Mann-Whitney test {#mann-whitney}

**The question:** Is pain 6 weeks after a midfoot injury different with a removable boot than with a cast?

### When to use it

- The outcome is **skewed**, has a **ceiling or floor**, or is **ordinal**, and you're comparing **two independent groups**.
- It asks whether values in one group tend to be **larger** than in the other: if you picked one patient from each group at random, how likely is the first to score higher?
- It's the same test as the **Wilcoxon rank-sum test**. R calls it `wilcox.test()`.
- If the outcome is roughly normal within each group → the [unpaired t test](#unpaired-t).

### Look at the data first

The trial measured pain on a numeric rating scale (NRS) from 0 (no pain) to 10 (the worst pain imaginable), in whole numbers: an **ordinal** scale.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

trial <- read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)   # one row per patient and visit

pain_6wk <- trial |>
  filter(visit == "6wk", !is.na(pain_nrs)) |>              # patients seen at 6 weeks
  mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("boot", "cast")))    # boot first: differences are boot minus cast

ggplot(pain_6wk, aes(pain_nrs)) +
  geom_bar() +                                             # one bar per whole score
  facet_wrap(~ arm, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(x = "Pain at 6 weeks (NRS, 0 = none, 10 = worst)", y = "Patients")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-two-unpaired-groups_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
pain_6wk |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median = median(pain_nrs),
            q1 = quantile(pain_nrs, 0.25), q3 = quantile(pain_nrs, 0.75))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  arm       n median    q1    q3
  <fct> <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 boot     58      4     3  4.75
2 cast     58      5     4  6   
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

trial = pd.read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv")                       # one row per patient and visit
pain_6wk = trial[trial["visit"] == "6wk"].dropna(subset=["pain_nrs"])     # patients seen at 6 weeks
pain_boot = pain_6wk.loc[pain_6wk["arm"] == "boot", "pain_nrs"]
pain_cast = pain_6wk.loc[pain_6wk["arm"] == "cast", "pain_nrs"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6, 4), sharex=True)
axes[0].hist(pain_boot, bins=np.arange(-0.5, 11))   # one bar per whole score
axes[0].set_title("boot")
axes[1].hist(pain_cast, bins=np.arange(-0.5, 11))
axes[1].set_title("cast")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Pain at 6 weeks (NRS, 0 = none, 10 = worst)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-two-unpaired-groups_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png)
:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(pain_6wk.groupby("arm")["pain_nrs"].describe()[["count", "25%", "50%", "75%"]])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      count  25%  50%   75%
arm                        
boot   58.0  3.0  4.0  4.75
cast   58.0  4.0  5.0  6.00
```


:::
:::

:::

Four patients missed the 6-week visit (2 in each arm), so 116 of the 120 randomized patients are analyzed. Most scores sit between 2 and 6, and many patients share a score (ties). With whole numbers on an ordinal scale, medians are the fair summary: 4 points with a boot and 5 with a cast.

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pain_test <- wilcox.test(pain_nrs ~ arm, data = pain_6wk,
                         exact = FALSE, correct = TRUE,   # see the R vs Python box
                         conf.int = TRUE)                 # adds the Hodges-Lehmann estimate and CI
pain_test
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  pain_nrs by arm
W = 1074.5, p-value = 0.0006596
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.9999535 -0.9999846
sample estimates:
difference in location 
             -1.000041 
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
# pg.mwu() runs scipy's Mann-Whitney test and adds the rank-biserial effect size
pain_test = pg.mwu(pain_boot, pain_cast, method="asymptotic", use_continuity=True)   # see the R vs Python box
print(pain_test)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      U_val alternative    p_val       RBC      CLES
MWU  1074.5   two-sided  0.00066 -0.361177  0.319411
```


:::
:::

:::





### Read the output

- **W = 1074.5** (R) or **U_val = 1074.5** (Python): the Mann-Whitney U statistic for the boot arm, the number of (boot, cast) pairs in which the boot patient reported more pain, counting ties as half. There are 58 × 58 = 3,364 pairs, so a U of 1,682 would mean no tendency either way. R calls it W.
- **p < 0.001:** a difference like this would be unusual if pain had the same distribution in both arms.
- **difference in location −1.00, 95% CI −2.00 to −1.00** (R only): the Hodges-Lehmann estimate, below. R finds it by a numerical search, so it prints −1.000041 and the like; the last digits are noise.
- **RBC = −0.361** (Python): the rank-biserial effect size, below.

### Effect size and 95% CI

- The **Hodges-Lehmann estimate** is the median of the differences between every boot patient's score and every cast patient's score: a typical difference, in points.
- The **rank-biserial correlation (r)** runs from −1 (every boot patient reported less pain than every cast patient) to +1 (the reverse). 0 means no tendency either way.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pain_test$estimate                                       # Hodges-Lehmann estimate, boot minus cast
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
difference in location 
             -1.000041 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
pain_test$conf.int                                       # its 95% CI
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -1.9999535 -0.9999846
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
effectsize::rank_biserial(pain_nrs ~ arm, data = pain_6wk)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
r (rank biserial) |         95% CI
----------------------------------
-0.36             | [-0.53, -0.17]
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
# Hodges-Lehmann estimate: the median of every boot-minus-cast difference
def hodges_lehmann(x, y):
    return np.median(np.subtract.outer(np.asarray(x), np.asarray(y)))

print(hodges_lehmann(pain_boot, pain_cast))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
-1.0
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
# scipy has no CI for it, so use a bootstrap: recompute it on 9999 resampled datasets.
# method="percentile": with whole-number scores, scipy's default method can't build this CI (see the R vs Python box)
hl_boot = stats.bootstrap((pain_boot.to_numpy(), pain_cast.to_numpy()), hodges_lehmann, vectorized=False,
                          method="percentile", rng=np.random.default_rng(2026))
print(hl_boot.confidence_interval)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
ConfidenceInterval(low=np.float64(-2.0), high=np.float64(-1.0))
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(pain_test["RBC"])                                  # rank-biserial r
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
MWU   -0.361177
Name: RBC, dtype: float64
```


:::
:::

:::





With a boot, pain was typically 1 point lower (95% CI 2 points to 1 point lower), and r = −0.36. Of all 3,364 (boot, cast) pairs, the boot patient reported less pain in 61%, more in 25%, and 14% were tied. With whole-number scores every difference between two patients is a whole number, so the Hodges-Lehmann estimate and its CI land on whole numbers too, and the estimate can sit on the edge of its own CI, as here.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** Pain at 6 weeks (NRS 0 to 10, an ordinal scale) was compared between the arms with the Mann-Whitney test, in the patients seen at that visit, with the Hodges-Lehmann estimate of the difference and its 95% CI as the effect size.
>
> **Results:** At 6 weeks, pain was a median of 4 points (IQR 3 to 4.75; n = 58) with a boot and 5 (IQR 4 to 6; n = 58) with a cast (Hodges-Lehmann difference −1 point, 95% CI −2 to −1; rank-biserial r = −0.36, 95% CI −0.53 to −0.17; p < 0.001).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: it isn't a test of medians
The Mann-Whitney test asks whether one group's values **tend to be larger**, not whether the medians differ. Two groups can have the same median and a significant Mann-Whitney test (if their shapes differ), or different medians and a non-significant one. Report the medians to describe the groups, but don't write "the medians differed significantly".
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: Mann-Whitney defaults
- **Exact or approximate.** With ties (as here) both programs use a normal approximation. Without ties, R computes an exact p-value for groups under 50, scipy only for very small groups. We set `exact = FALSE` in R and `method="asymptotic"` in Python so they always match.
- **Continuity correction.** Both programs apply it by default for the approximation; we set it explicitly anyway.
- **The Hodges-Lehmann CI.** R computes it by inverting the test; the Python code uses a bootstrap, a different method. With whole-number scores the estimate barely moves: leaving out any one patient still gives −1. scipy's default bootstrap method (BCa) needs those leave-one-out estimates to vary, so here it returns `nan` with a warning. The percentile method (`method="percentile"`) doesn't need them. Here the two CIs agree (−2.00 to −1.00); on other data they can differ a little.
:::

## Fisher's exact test and chi-square {#fisher-chi-square}

**The question:** Is graft failure within 2 years of an ACL reconstruction more common with a hamstring graft than with a bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB) graft?

### When to use it

- The outcome is **yes/no**, compared between **two independent groups**: a 2 × 2 table.
- **Fisher's exact test** is valid for any sample size. The **chi-square test** is a large-sample approximation: use it only when every *expected* count is at least 5. When in doubt, use Fisher's test.
- If patients were followed for different lengths of time and the event can happen at any time → the [log-rank test](#log-rank).

### Look at the data first

The ACL data hold one row per primary reconstruction. Everyone was followed for at least 2 years unless the graft failed first, so failure within 2 years (`failure_2y`) is known for every reconstruction. For two yes/no variables, "looking" means the 2 × 2 table, with the percentage in each group.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

acl <- read_csv("data/acl_cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
two_grafts <- acl |> filter(graft %in% c("hamstring", "BPTB"))   # the question compares two of the three grafts

# Put the comparison group first and the outcome "yes" first
failure_table <- table(
  graft  = factor(two_grafts$graft, levels = c("hamstring", "BPTB")),
  failed = factor(two_grafts$failure_2y, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("yes", "no"))
)
failure_table
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
           failed
graft       yes  no
  hamstring   6 148
  BPTB        6 123
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
prop.table(failure_table, margin = 1)    # row percentages: failures with each graft
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
           failed
graft              yes         no
  hamstring 0.03896104 0.96103896
  BPTB      0.04651163 0.95348837
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from scipy.stats.contingency import odds_ratio
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import confint_proportions_2indep

acl = pd.read_csv("data/acl_cohort.csv")
two_grafts = acl[acl["graft"].isin(["hamstring", "BPTB"])]   # the question compares two of the three grafts

# Put the comparison group first and the outcome "yes" (1) first
failure_table = pd.crosstab(two_grafts["graft"], two_grafts["failure_2y"]).loc[["hamstring", "BPTB"], [1, 0]]
print(failure_table)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

graft

BPTB        6  123
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(pd.crosstab(two_grafts["graft"], two_grafts["failure_2y"], normalize="index"))   # row percentages
```

```

graft

```

6 of 154 hamstring grafts (3.9%) and 6 of 129 BPTB grafts (4.7%) failed within 2 years.

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
failure_fisher <- fisher.test(failure_table)
failure_fisher
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  failure_table
p-value = 0.7754
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.2163564 3.1962761
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
 0.8316302 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
chisq.test(failure_table)$expected       # all at least 5, so chi-square is also fine
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
           failed
graft            yes     no
  hamstring 6.530035 147.47
  BPTB      5.469965 123.53
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
failure_chisq <- chisq.test(failure_table)
failure_chisq
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  failure_table
X-squared = 0.00031649, df = 1, p-value = 0.9858
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
failure_fisher = stats.fisher_exact(failure_table)
print(failure_fisher.pvalue)
```

### Read the output

- **Fisher's test, p-value = 0.7754:** a table like this would be common if failure were unrelated to the graft. We report it as p = 0.775.
- **odds ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.22 to 3.20** (R): the effect size, below.
- **Expected counts:** what each cell would hold if failure were unrelated to the graft. All are at least 5, but only just (the smallest is 5.5), so the chi-square test is valid too.
- **X-squared = 0.0003, p-value = 0.986:** the chi-square test, with Yates' continuity correction, agrees.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Under the hood: Yates' continuity correction
The chi-square test treats counts as if they could take any value, but counts are whole numbers. For a 2 × 2 table, **Yates' correction** subtracts 0.5 from each |observed − expected| difference before squaring, which makes the p-value larger (more cautious). It's meant to bring the p-value closer to Fisher's, but it can overshoot, as here: each observed count is only about half a count from its expected count (6 failures against 6.5 and 5.5 expected), so the corrected statistic is almost 0 and p = 0.986, against Fisher's 0.775. Both R's `chisq.test()` and scipy's `chi2_contingency()` apply it to 2 × 2 tables by default; without it (`correct = FALSE`, `correction=False`) p = 0.754. Either is acceptable if you say which you used; with small counts, prefer Fisher's test.
:::

### Effect size and 95% CI

Two effect sizes, and it's worth reporting both:

- The **risk difference**: the difference between the two percentages, in percentage points. It's what patients and clinicians understand.
- The **odds ratio**: the odds of failure with a hamstring graft divided by the odds with a BPTB graft. It's what logistic regression reports ([page 11](11-predict-from-one.qmd#logistic-regression)), so it's useful for comparing with other studies.

>

The odds ratio's CI runs from 0.22 to 3.20: the data are compatible with a hamstring graft having a fifth of the odds of failure of a BPTB graft, or three times the odds. ## 🔀 R vs Python: two different odds ratios

R's `fisher.test()` reports the **conditional maximum-likelihood** odds ratio, 0.8316, which goes with its exact CI. Use `scipy.stats.contingency.odds_ratio(..., kind="conditional")` to get R's number and CI. The two are always close; say which you report.
:::

## Log-rank test {#log-rank}

**The question:** Is revision-free survival different between implant A and implant C?

### When to use it

- The outcome is **time until an event** (revision), patients were followed for different lengths of time, and you're comparing **two independent groups**.
- It compares the whole survival curves, not the survival at one time point.
- The **Mantel-Haenszel test** (or Mantel-Cox test) in the decision table is the same test under another name.
- It's most powerful when one group's risk is a steady multiple of the other's over time (proportional hazards). If the curves cross, see [page 14](../survival/14-cox-regression.qmd#proportional-hazards).
- To compare three or more groups, or to adjust for other variables → [Cox regression](08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#cox).

### Look at the data first

```{.r .cell-code}

library(ggsurvfit)

  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  scale_ggsurvfit() +
  labs(x = "Years since surgery", y = "Revision-free survival")
```

### How to report it

> **Methods:** Revision-free survival was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method and compared between implants with the log-rank test. Hazard ratios were estimated with Cox proportional hazards regression.
>
> **Results:** Revision-free survival at 5 years was 71.1% (95% CI 61.5% to 78.8%) with implant C and 89.9% (95% CI 84.7% to 93.3%) with implant A (log-rank p < 0.001; hazard ratio 3.04, 95% CI 1.83 to 5.04).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: overlapping CIs aren't a test
Comparing the two curves' CIs at one time point ("the 5-year CIs overlap, so there's no difference") isn't a valid test, and neither is comparing the crude percentages revised. Use the log-rank test on the whole curves. And as on [page 4](04-describe-one-group.qmd#kaplan-meier), deaths here are treated as censored; [page 13](../survival/13-kaplan-meier.qmd#competing-risks) covers competing risks.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: one formula or two groups
R's `survdiff()` takes a formula with a grouping variable. lifelines' `logrank_test()` takes each group's follow-up times and events separately (`multivariate_logrank_test()` takes a grouping column). They compute the same test. Both Cox models handle tied revision times with Efron's method, so the hazard ratios agree.
:::
